Bhai Dooj

Diwali Bedtime Stories · Book 7 · A Story Before Sleep

Bhai Dooj

भाई दूज

The day a sister's tilak melted even Yama

Before Sleep · · सोने से पहले

This story is for bedtime — slowly, like warm milk. Where the talk sits in a yellow box, read it in different voices — children remember that part best of all. Where you see chhan-chhan, let it sound like bangles; where you see tan-tan, let the aarti bell ring.

This is the story of the last night of the Diwali week — the night when a brother who keeps the accounts of every life came to his sister's home as a guest. And his sister marked his forehead with tilak, fed him with her own hands, and asked for a blessing that is still celebrated in every home today.

If your eyes grow heavy as you listen, it does not matter — stories do their work even in half-sleep. Tomorrow morning, when you meet your brother or sister, this story will come back to you — and maybe a smile with it.

The People of the Story · · कहानी के लोग

Yama — son of the Sun. Keeper of the accounts of all deeds, lord of justice. But in this story he is only a brother — a brother who has not visited his sister's home for years.

Yamuna — daughter of the Sun, Yama's twin sister. The goddess who flows as a river, and the very image of affection. Her home stands by the riverbank, and her heart has always been open to her brother.

Chitragupta — Yama's record-keeper. In his ledger every deed of every life is written — the good ones too, and the bad ones. He does his work smiling, never stern.

Surya — the father. In whose golden palace both children grew up, and from whose courtyard both set out on their own paths.

And you — the sisters and brothers of today, in whose homes this festival is celebrated every year. This story belongs to them.

When We Celebrate · · कब मनाते हैं

Kartik Shukla Dwitiya

Bhai Dooj is celebrated two days after Diwali, on the second day (dwitiya) of the bright half of the month of Kartik. In 2026: 11 November in India, 10 November in America.

The Diwali week begins with Dhanteras, passes through the dawn of Narakasura's end, glows with Ayodhya's lamps, welcomes Lakshmi, Govardhan and Bali's visit, and at last arrives at Bhai Dooj. It is the week's final link — and perhaps its tenderest.

The Sun's Twins · · सूरज के जुड़वाँ बच्चे

A very long time ago, in the Sun's golden palace, two children grew up together — a boy and a girl, twins. The boy's name was Yama, the girl's Yami — whom everyone later called Yamuna. They were like each other's shadows: where Yama went, Yami went with him; where Yami laughed, Yama broke into a smile.

Then one day each received their own work. Yama received the work of justice — keeping the accounts of all deeds, and holding the scales of dharma straight. Yami received the work of flowing as a river — watering the fields, quenching thirst, washing sorrows away. Both took up their work, but both their hearts stayed with each other.

Little Yama — 'Sister, my work will take me far away, but I will never forget you.'

Little Yami — 'Then promise me — every year on this day you will come to my home. I will mark your tilak, feed you, and you will not refuse.'

Pause and think — When a brother and sister live far apart, how great is the promise to meet? Have you ever made such a promise to your brother or sister?

The Invitation, Again and Again · · बुलावा, बार-बार

Years passed. Yamuna lived in her home by the riverbank, and every year, as soon as Kartik's dwitiya arrived, she sent her brother an invitation — sometimes by the wind, sometimes by a traveller's hand, sometimes with a garland of flowers. And every year the same answer came back: 'Sister, there is so much work. The ledger never ends.'

And it was true. At Yama's door someone arrived every moment — one account closing, another beginning. In Chitragupta's ledger a new name joined every instant. Even if Yama had wished it, he could not rise. But his sister's invitation burned in his heart like a diya — it never went out.

Chitragupta — 'Lord, the ledger never ends. A hundred names remain today.'

Yama — 'I know, friend. But my sister's invitation never ends either.'

Pause and think — When someone is very busy, making time to meet is itself love. Have you ever persuaded a busy loved one to come and meet you?

The Brother Arrives · · भाई का आना

Then one year, the dawn of Kartik Shukla Dwitiya arrived. Yamuna decorated the door — marigold garlands, mango leaves, and diyas in every corner. The aarti plate was ready, the bowl of sweets was ready, and her heart — her heart had been ready for so long. Then came a sound at the door. Tan-tan — as if someone had knocked softly.

Yamuna opened the door, and there he was — brother! The same face, the same smile, but this time no hurry, no ledger. Yama smiled and said, 'Sister, this time no work came between us.' And Yamuna's eyes filled — with joy, after years of waiting.

Then came the moment for which this day is known. Yamuna seated her brother, marked his forehead with red tilak — to the chhan-chhan of her bangles — waved the aarti, and sweetened his mouth. Yama closed his eyes and felt that tilak, as if years of weariness lifted in a single moment.

Yamuna — 'Brother, you have come! Today I will not let you go anywhere.'

Yama — 'Today I will not go anywhere either, sister. Today belongs only to you.'

Pause and think — Why does a home light up when a loved one arrives? Is it the light of the diyas, or the light of the heart?

A Meal from Sister's Hands · · बहन के हाथ का खाना

After the tilak, Yamuna served her brother food cooked with her own hands — hot, fresh, and so much that the plate overflowed. They sat and ate together, and as they ate, childhood memories poured out — floating leaf-boats on the river, racing down the steps of the Sun's palace, and the day little Yama plucked a mango and gave it to Yami first.

Yama was laughing — not as a god laughs, but as a little brother laughs. The ledger, the accounts, justice — all of it stayed far away for a while. Only a brother and sister remained, one plate, and laughter years old.

Yama — 'Sister, it has been years since I ate food from your hands.'

Yamuna — 'Then eat your fill today, brother — today no ledger will come between us.'

Pause and think — Feeding someone with your own hands is itself a kind of love. In your home, who feeds whom with their own hands?

The Boon · · वरदान

When the meal was done and both sat at ease, Yama said, 'Sister, today you have given me so much — now it is my turn. Ask, what do you want?' Yamuna smiled. She asked nothing for herself — no gold, no palace, no jewel. She said, 'Brother, give only one promise — that a brother whom his sister marks with tilak on this day shall never be touched by untimely death, and that every sister shall always be happy.'

Yama looked at his sister for a moment, then said softly, 'So be it.' And he gave his sister a gift as well — a garland of flowers that never fade, which graces Yamuna's home to this day. They say that from that very day the promise entered every home: a sister's tilak became a brother's protection.

Yama — 'Sister, ask — today every word of yours is my command.'

Yamuna — 'Then listen, brother — my blessing is for everyone. A brother marked by his sister's tilak shall live long; and every sister's home shall hold happiness.'

Pause and think — Yamuna asked nothing for herself — asking for others is the greatest asking of all. What would you ask for someone else?

Chitragupta's Ledger · · चित्रगुप्त की बही

Meanwhile, somewhere else, another smile was blooming. Chitragupta — who always lives with his ledger — had set his pen down that day and was smiling. For his sister's blessing had given his ledger a holiday too: today no name would be struck off; today only blessings would be written.

That is why on Bhai Dooj, pen, ink-pot and ledger are also worshipped — especially in homes where accounts are life itself. People offer flowers to their pens, bow to their books, and remember that good deeds are written in letters of gold.

Chitragupta — 'The lord's sister has given my ledger a holiday too. Today I will write only blessings.'

Pause and think — If there were a ledger of your deeds, what would be written in it today? And what would you wish to have written in it tomorrow?

To Every Home · · हर घर तक

Even after Yama left, that day did not stop there. The custom that left Yamuna's home slowly reached every home — first the neighbourhood, then the town, then the whole country. Today every sister calls her brother, marks his tilak, waves the aarti, feeds him, and the brother gives his sister a gift.

And this love is celebrated under different names too — in Bengal it is called Bhai Phonta, in Maharashtra Bhau Beej. Different names, but the same thing: a sister's tilak, a brother's protection, and the love between them.

A sister today — 'Brother, come — let me mark your tilak!'

A brother today — 'Coming, sister! Today no work will come between us.'

Pause and think — When does one home's story become a whole country's story? Perhaps when everyone sees their own home in it.

Why It Matters · · क्यों

Now think — who is Yama? He before whom every account opens, from whom no one escapes. And that very Yama was melted by a sister's tilak. That is why this story is so beloved: it tells us that love is greater than any account, and affection softer even than justice.

And this is not the only story. In these very Diwali books you have already met Yama three times — Karva stood before him with courage and asked for her husband; the bride of Hima's son stopped him at the door with the light of her lamps; and now Yamuna has melted him with love. Three times, three strengths of women — courage, cleverness, and love — and all three times Yama bowed, not defeated, but made human.

Pause and think — Is love truly greater even than death? What is this story's answer — and what is yours?

At Home · · घर पर कैसे

  • The sister marks her brother's tilak, waves the aarti, and feeds him sweets.
  • The brother gives his sister a gift — and they sit and eat together, refreshing old memories.
  • If you can, remember the Yamuna river; if no river is near, light a diya and pray for the protection of brothers and sisters.
  • In Chitragupta's memory, honour pen and book — one who reads and writes is also writing their own deeds.
  • And at the end — embrace each other and say: 'Next year again, on this very day, at this very door.'

Pause and think — Tonight before sleeping, say a good prayer in your heart for your brother or sister — silently, without telling anyone. That is this story's truest worship.

Good night — and tomorrow, when you meet your brother or sister, be sure to give them a tilak-smile.

Words to Know · · शब्दार्थ

  • Tilak — the auspicious mark on the forehead; a symbol of blessing and protection.
  • Dwitiya — the second day of a lunar fortnight; Bhai Dooj falls on Kartik Shukla Dwitiya.
  • Yama — son of the Sun, lord of the accounts of deeds and of justice.
  • Chitragupta — Yama's record-keeper, in whose ledger every deed is written.
  • Bahi — a book of accounts; here, the book of deeds.
  • Boon (vardaan) — a promise or blessing given by a god.
  • Aarti — honour offered with the flame of a diya.
  • Bhai Phonta — Bhai Dooj's name in Bengal.
  • Bhau Beej — Bhai Dooj's name in Maharashtra.
  • Yamuna — daughter of the Sun, Yama's twin sister, and a sacred river.

Sources · · स्रोत

Yama and Yami (Yamuna) are the twin children of the Sun — their dialogue is found in the Rigveda's Yama-Yami hymn (10.10). This book begins from that ancient bond.

The tale of Yama's visit to Yamuna's home, the tilak and the boon on Bhai Dooj is told far and wide. It is not tied here to any single verse or chapter — it is a tale of folk tradition, told in that form.

Chitragupta is known in Puranic tradition as Yama's record-keeper; the worship of pen, ink-pot and ledger on Bhai Dooj is a living Kayastha tradition.

Bhai Phonta in Bengal and Bhau Beej in Maharashtra — the same festival under different names — is living tradition.

Date: Kartik Shukla Dwitiya; in 2026, 11 November in India, 10 November in America.

Yama has deliberately been kept gentle in this story — for a bedtime tale, the brother's form was chosen, not the fearsome form of the lord of justice.
